stops.accessibility: Level stone pavement on the bridge itself; the lakeside approaches are flat and step free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open lakeside, no ticket and no gate. Verify locally only if arriving very late, when the area lighting dims.
stops.insiderTip: Come back in snow if you ever can: the famous lingering-snow view happens because sun melts the south-facing slope first, leaving one white arc that looks snapped in half.
stops.name: Broken Bridge (Duanqiao)
stops.narration:
Start at the north-east corner of the lake, where a low stone arch hops a narrow outlet and half of Hangzhou seems to be taking the same photograph. This is Duanqiao, the Broken Bridge, and nothing about it is broken.

The name is a weather trick. Duanqiao Canxue — lingering snow on the Broken Bridge — is one of the Ten Views of West Lake, a set of famous scenes named and inscribed by emperors centuries ago. After snow, the bridge's south-facing slope melts in the sun while the shaded side stays white, so from the shore the arch looks snapped in two. The bridge is whole; the snow draws the crack.

The other half of the fame is a love story. The legend of the White Snake — one of China's four great folk tales — says Xu Xian, an ordinary young man, met the beautiful White Snake spirit on this bridge in the rain, lent her his umbrella, and married her. She was a thousand-year-old serpent who had taken human form out of gratitude, and the tale follows her through jealousy, magic, floods and a vengeful monk. Opera troupes still perform it; every Chinese schoolchild knows the umbrella. You are standing on literature's most famous first date.

Look one way for the umbrella crowds and the other for Baochu Pagoda, the thin grey tower on the hill behind you — a pagoda being a tiered Buddhist tower, this one first raised a thousand years ago. No ticket here, open lakeside at all hours. Take your photo, then walk.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west off the bridge onto Bai Causeway, the tree-lined embankment running along the water. Follow it about 500 metres to the open viewing terrace with the stone tablet. That is the next stop.
stops.openingHours: Open lakeside at all hours; best in daylight, roughly 07:00 to 22:00 for the lit evening scene.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Suicasmo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Flat paved embankment, fully step free and kind to wheels, though crowded at weekends.
stops.insiderTip: November is this causeway's best month: the plane trees go gold and the gingkoes drop yellow fans on the path, and the morning mist sits on the water until about nine.
stops.name: Bai Causeway (Baidi)
stops.narration:
You are walking on a poem's infrastructure. This embankment is named for Bai Juyi, the Tang-dynasty poet who governed Hangzhou in 822 — a dynasty being a line of emperors from one family, the Tang ruling China from 618 to 907. Bai ordered the lake dredged and an embankment raised so farmers got irrigation and the city got a road. Twelve centuries later you are strolling his public works.

Stop at the terrace with the stone tablet: Pinghu Qiuyue, the Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake, another of the Ten Views. The idea behind the Ten Views matters more than any single one. Emperors and poets picked the lake's best angles, built pavilions on them and wrote their names in stone, turning scenery into a text the whole country learned to read. West Lake is not just pretty water; it is a landscape edited by a thousand years of critics, which is exactly why UNESCO listed it in 2011 — not as wilderness but as a cultural landscape, a place where human design and nature improved each other.

In November the design shows off. The London plane trees lining the path turn the colour of weak tea, gingkoes — ancient fan-leaved trees that outlived the dinosaurs — drop yellow confetti, and the maples redden behind them. No ticket, no gate, just keep walking west toward the wooded hill rising from the water.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue west to the end of the causeway, then follow the lakeside path south about 1.2 kilometres toward the wooded island-hill. Cross the small bridge onto it. The scholar gardens at its heart are the next stop.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily at all hours.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 钉钉, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Gentle slopes with some steps between garden terraces; the main paths are manageable but not fully step free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The hill park is free to enter. Small exhibition halls may ask a nominal fee; verify locally.
stops.insiderTip: Eat lunch at Lou Wai Lou on the hill's south shore if there is a table: its Dongpo pork — slow-braised cubes named for the poet you meet at the next stop — is the dish Hangzhou argues about.
stops.name: Solitary Hill (Gushan)
stops.narration:
Cross the little bridge and you step off the mainland entirely. Gushan, Solitary Hill, is the lake's largest island, and for a thousand years it has been where Hangzhou's scholars came to think.

The thought took physical form in 1904, when a group of seal carvers founded the Xiling Seal Art Society here — China's first scholarly society for the art of the seal, meaning the carved stone stamp pressed in red ink beside calligraphy. A seal looks trivial until you learn the mechanism: carving two characters backwards into stone, in an ancient script, so they print forwards in a square centimetre, is scholarship, craft and identity in one object. The society's founders believed these little stones carried the soul of Chinese writing, and they built pavilions, ponds and bamboo groves to argue about them in. Walk the grounds slowly; the graves of scholars and the quiet pools are the point, not any single building.

The small stone pagoda in your photograph is the Huayanjing stupa on the hill's flank — one of several old towers tucked in the trees. The hill park itself is free, with small halls sometimes asking a nominal fee, so verify locally. From here the walk turns south toward the lake's longest embankment.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the island by Xiling Bridge on the south side and follow the lakeside path south about 1.8 kilometres to the willow-lined causeway stretching down the lake. The statue of the bearded poet at its northern end marks the next stop.
stops.openingHours: Open daily in daylight hours, roughly 07:00 to 18:00; verify locally in winter.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: jaaron, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Flat paved causeway, fully step free; the bridge arches have gentle ramps and low steps at some crossings.
stops.insiderTip: Count the six arched bridges as you walk: each frames a different postcard — lake east, hills west — and the third from the north gives the classic pagoda-across-water shot.
stops.name: Su Causeway (Sudi)
stops.narration:
Meet the man this 2.8-kilometre embankment is named for. The bronze figure at the causeway's head is Su Shi, also called Su Dongpo — poet, essayist, official, and the most beloved writer China ever produced — who governed Hangzhou in 1089.

Here is what he did, and it is gloriously practical. West Lake was choking on silt and weeds, which meant no irrigation, no drinking water and no beauty. Su mobilized the dredging gangs, scooped the lake clean, and piled the mud into this long embankment planted with willows and hibiscus, crossed by six arched bridges. A flood-control project that doubled as a promenade: that is the whole West Lake philosophy in one gesture, and the Spring Dawn on Su Causeway — mist, willow floss, orioles — became the first of the Ten Views.

Su also gave Hangzhou its signature dish. Legend says he distributed slow-braised pork to the dredging workers, and Dongpo pork — red-cooked, sweet, collapsing cubes — still sits on every banquet menu. Poetry you can eat. Walk the full causeway south; it is about a kilometre to the garden at its foot, willows one side, open water the other, and in November the leaves do half the entertaining.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south down the full length of the causeway about a kilometre to its southern end, then step into the garden of pavilions and fish ponds on the right. That is the next stop.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily at all hours.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: joiseyshowaa, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Level garden paths, mostly step free; pond edges are low-walled and watchful with children.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public park, no ticket. Fish food pellets cost a few yuan at kiosks.
stops.insiderTip: Buy the cheapest bag of fish food at a kiosk: the moment pellets hit the water the pond boils red, and that churning crowd is the park's most honest spectacle.
stops.name: Flower Harbor (Huagang Guanyu)
stops.narration:
Step off the causeway into the smell of osmanthus and fish food. Huagang Guanyu — viewing fish at the flower harbor — began as a private garden of a Southern Song official and hardened into another of the Ten Views: red carp boiling in a clear pond under peonies and maples.

Watch the water first. The carp mob the edges because generations of visitors have trained them: food falls here, so they wait here, a thousand orange mouths in a learned queue. It is funny and a little unsettling — a wild animal reshaped by snacks — and the park leans in, selling pellets for a few yuan so you can join the conditioning.

Then lift your eyes to the hills behind the garden, because that green slope is Hangzhou's other economy. Those terraces grow Longjing, Dragon Well tea — flat-pressed green leaves, pan-fired by hand in hot woks, that brew pale gold and sell at eye-watering prices. Leaves picked before Qingming, the tomb-sweeping festival in early April, fetch the most, and villages like Meijiawu in the hills live off the spring rush of pickers and tasting-room tourists. The national tea museum sits just uphill across the road if you want the full story; the garden itself is free, no ticket. From here you head east to the pagoda on the hill.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the garden by its eastern gate and follow the lakeside road east about 1.1 kilometres toward the tall ochre pagoda on the hill. Enter through the ticket gate at its base. That is the next stop.
stops.openingHours: Open daily in daylight hours, roughly 07:00 to 21:00; verify locally by season.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: lienyuan lee, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Bluntly easy for a pagoda: escalators climb the hill and elevators serve every storey, so wheels and tired knees reach the top. Some thresholds at the terraces.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed scenic area: about 40 yuan at last check. Verify prices at the gate; they are revised without warning.
stops.insiderTip: Ride to the top near sunset: the lake turns pewter, the causeways you walked draw two dark lines across it, and Baochu Pagoda answers from the northern hill.
stops.name: Leifeng Pagoda
stops.narration:
Climb — by escalator, gloriously — to the ochre tower on Thunder Peak Hill. A pagoda is a tiered Buddhist tower, part reliquary and part landmark, and this one's biography is pure Hangzhou melodrama.

The first Leifeng Pagoda went up in 975 under a king of Wuyue, the regional kingdom that ruled this coast before China reunified. It held Buddhist relics and watched the lake for 950 years. Then, in the early 1900s, treasure hunters and the superstitious picked its bricks apart — people believed the tower's clay warded off illness — until the hollowed shell collapsed in 1924 with a crash the whole city heard. What you see now is the 2002 rebuild: steel frame, five glowing storeys, escalators up the hill and elevators inside, keeping the old silhouette with new bones. Purists sniff; your knees will not.

The legend clings anyway. Under this hill, the White Snake tale says, the vengeful monk imprisoned the White Lady herself — true love sealed under stone. Entry costs about 40 yuan, China's currency, at last check, but verify at the gate. Ride to the top gallery and read the lake you just walked: two causeways stitching the water, the island-hill, the tea slopes behind. Then come down, because the last stop is not walkable and that is honest.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the honest ride, not a stroll: Lingyin Temple sits 6 kilometres north-west — over an hour and a half on foot along trafficked roads — so do not walk it. Take a taxi or ride-hailing car from the pagoda car park, about 25 minutes, or a lakeside bus toward Lingyin. Allow about an hour door to door with the temple queues.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 08:00 to 17:30 in the low season and later in summer. Verify at the gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Tyg728, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Long uphill approach with steps and crowds; the halls have high thresholds. Wheelchair users will need help and should expect a demanding visit.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Two tickets: the Feilai Feng grottoes area about 45 yuan plus the temple itself about 30 yuan at last check. Budget around 75 yuan combined and verify every price at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the laughing Maitreya carved into the Feilai Feng cliff before you enter: belly out, grin wide, sack of troubles over his shoulder — the future Buddha as a travelling optimist.
stops.name: Lingyin Temple
stops.narration:
You arrive through a valley of stone smiles. Feilai Feng, the Peak That Flew Here, is a limestone crag covered in more than three hundred Buddhist carvings cut under the Song and Yuan dynasties — the Yuan being the Mongol emperors who ruled China from 1271 to 1368. The grinning giant among them is Maitreya, the Buddha of the future, shown as a fat laughing monk: Buddhism's promise that enlightenment can look like joy, not severity.

Buddhism is the Indian-born faith that suffering comes from craving and can be ended by practice, and it reached Hangzhou early. An Indian monk named Huili founded this temple in 328, naming it Lingyin, the Retreat of the Soul, and it grew into one of China's great Chan temples — Chan being the meditation school the Japanese call Zen. Inside the halls, the line of guardians gives way to the Great Hall's vast Sakyamuni, the historical Buddha, flanked by the great bodhisattvas — a bodhisattva being an enlightened being who stays behind to rescue others, with Guanyin, the goddess of mercy, the most beloved of all. Incense smoke, chanting, donation QR codes: seventeen centuries of devotion running on modern rails.

Expect two tickets totalling around 75 yuan, China's currency, at last check — verify at the gate — and real crowds by mid-morning. The approach is uphill with steps and high thresholds, so take it slowly.

End of the walk. Tomorrow, chase the tea: ride up to Meijiawu village in the hills for picking-season tastings and farm lunches, and spend your last evening on Hefang Street, the old lane below the hill, eating your way past sesame cakes and pian-er-chuan noodles. Heaven below, full stomach included.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Buses and taxis leave from the temple car park back to the lake and the city; in the evening, ask for Hefang Street for dinner and the old-lane stroll.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 07:00 to 18:00; the grottoes close earlier in winter. Verify at the gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Tyg728, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start by 08:30 on a November weekday: mist on the water, tour buses still parking, gingkoes lit gold. Weekends clog the causeways by ten. Afternoon light fades fast; be off the lake by 16:30 and save Lingyin for the second morning.
tour.difficulty: Easy and flat around the lake — about 5.6 km of paved causeways and garden paths, roughly eighty-five minutes of walking — plus one bus or taxi hop to Lingyin Temple, where the approach is uphill with steps.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.
tour.overviewText:
There is an old Chinese saying that paradise in heaven has a twin on earth, and its name is Hangzhou. Stand on the Broken Bridge on a November morning, mist combing the willows and a gold gingko leaf landing on your sleeve, and the boast stops sounding like boasting.

Hangzhou matters because it has been rich, holy and beautiful for a very long time, all at once. In 1127 the Song court — a dynasty being one family's line of emperors, and the Song among China's great ones — fled invasion and made this lakeside town its capital, Lin'an. For a century and a half the biggest city on earth sat here: silk merchants, poets, painters and officials packed inside walls whose lake-facing gates opened onto scenery the emperors personally edited. That habit never left. The West Lake you walk today is a designed landscape — causeways raised by poet-governors, viewpoints named in imperial calligraphy — and UNESCO listed it in 2011 for exactly that: a cultural landscape where nature and human craft spent a thousand years improving each other.

Two economies still run on that beauty. Up in the hills behind the lake, villages like Meijiawu grow Longjing, Dragon Well tea — leaves pan-pressed flat by hand in hot woks, the pickings from before the early-April Qingming festival worth a fortune — and spring turns the slopes into a carnival of pickers and tasting rooms. Down in the valley, Buddhism pays its own way: Lingyin Temple, founded in 328 by an Indian monk, draws millions of pilgrims and incense-buyers a year to burn sticks before the great laughing Buddhas. Tea money and temple smoke, scholar seals and poetry menus — and underneath, a modern tech metropolis of over ten million people that built its fortune on e-commerce and still introduces itself by its lake.

The shape of the walk is simple. You start at the Broken Bridge, trace the lake's two great historic causeways south past gardens and an island of scholars to Leifeng Pagoda — a pagoda being a tiered Buddhist tower — covering about five and a half kilometres on foot, roughly eighty-five minutes of walking. Then you ride out to Lingyin Temple in the western hills, because the honest 6 kilometres are trafficked roads no walker wants.

November practicals: this is the lake's finest month. Plane trees gold, gingkoes yellow, maples red, mist most mornings, daytime highs often in the mid-teens Celsius — bring layers and start early, since tour groups and weekend crowds thicken by ten. The pagoda and temple charge in yuan, China's currency, around 40 and 75 respectively; verify every price at the gate, carry cash for park kiosks, and expect sunset to end sightseeing by five.

Bring an empty morning and comfortable shoes. The lake has waited a thousand years to show off; it can wait for you to finish your tea.
tour.summary: West Lake in autumn gold: two poet-built causeways, a scholar's island, a rebuilt pagoda and a great Buddhist temple, with one honest ride to the hills.
tour.title: Hangzhou – West Lake & Tea Hills
